body: (a) List the elements of **prime cost**. (b) Explain (i) cost unit; (ii) cost centre. (c) List **three** ways costs are analysed according to **function**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** Prime cost = **direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses**.
>
> **(b)(i)** A **cost unit** is a **unit of product or service** in relation to which costs are ascertained and expressed (e.g. per tonne, per metre, per passenger-km, per bed-night).
>
> **(ii)** A **cost centre** is a **location, person, function or item of equipment** for which costs are collected and charged (e.g. machining department, canteen, a machine).
>
> **(c)** **Production (factory) costs**; **administration costs**; **selling and distribution costs**; (also research and development, finance costs).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Prime cost excludes all overheads.

## Simplified explanation

Direct materials + labour + expenses.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: Explain the procedure for the preparation of a **budget**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. **Set objectives/policies** of the organisation for the budget period.
> 2. Set up a **budget committee** and appoint a **budget officer**; issue a **budget manual**.
> 3. Identify the **principal (limiting) budget factor**, e.g. sales demand, materials, labour or capacity.
> 4. Prepare the **sales budget** (usually first), then the **functional budgets**: production, materials, labour, overheads, administration, selling, capital expenditure.
> 5. **Coordinate** and review the functional budgets; negotiate revisions.
> 6. Prepare the **cash budget** and **master budget** (budgeted income statement and statement of financial position).
> 7. **Approve** and communicate the budget to managers.
> 8. **Monitor**: compare actual with budget regularly, analyse variances and take corrective action (budgetary control).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Emphasise the principal budget factor and the master budget.

## Simplified explanation

Objectives → committee → limiting factor → sales budget → functional → master → control.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: (a) What is **standard costing**? (b) Explain the following variances: (i) direct material cost variance; (ii) direct labour cost variance.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** Standard costing is a control technique in which **predetermined (standard) costs** for materials, labour and overheads are set for each unit, and **actual costs are compared with them** to find **variances**, which are analysed and acted upon.
>
> **(b)(i)** **Direct material cost variance** = standard cost of materials for actual output − actual cost of materials = **(SQ × SP) − (AQ × AP)**. It splits into a **price** variance (SP − AP) × AQ and a **usage** variance (SQ − AQ) × SP.
>
> **(ii)** **Direct labour cost variance** = standard labour cost for actual output − actual labour cost = **(SH × SR) − (AH × AR)**. It splits into a **rate** variance (SR − AR) × AH and an **efficiency** variance (SH − AH) × SR.
>
> A positive result (actual < standard) is **favourable**; a negative one is **adverse**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Show the formulae and sub-variances.

## Simplified explanation

Standards vs actuals; price/usage and rate/efficiency.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: (a) What is **process costing**? (b) State **three** features of process costing.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** Process costing is a method of costing used where **identical units are produced continuously through a sequence of processes**; costs are accumulated **for each process** and averaged over the units produced (e.g. oil refining, cement, textiles, food processing).
>
> **(b)** Features: (1) **continuous, mass production** of homogeneous units; (2) costs are collected **by process/department**; (3) the **output of one process is the input of the next**; (4) **normal and abnormal losses** (and gains) arise and are accounted for; (5) **work-in-progress** is valued using **equivalent units**; (6) joint products and by-products may arise.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Contrast with job costing, where each job is costed separately.

## Simplified explanation

Continuous identical units; cost per process; losses and equivalent units.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body:
Bouloko and Sons uses a plastic component. Stock on 1 January 2007 was **13,800 units at D46** each.

Receipts: 2 Jan 4,600 @ D48; 5 Feb 1,800 @ D49; 6 Mar 3,800 @ D50; 27 Mar 2,900 @ D51.

Issues: 9 Jan 9,200; 25 Jan 3,600; 10 Feb 3,200; 18 Feb 3,400; 29 Mar 3,800 units.

Issues are priced at **weighted average cost**. Prepare the stores ledger account.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Weighted average smooths price changes; the average changes only when new stock is received at a different price.

## Simplified explanation

Average after each receipt; issue at that average.
hint: Recompute the average price after each receipt.

body:
Johannes Textiles Co. Ltd, year ended 31 December 2006: production and sales **4,000 metres** at **N25** per metre.

Costs (N): direct materials 18,000; wages: fixed 6,000, variable 8,000; factory overhead: fixed 2,000, variable 8,000; establishment charges: fixed 6,000, variable 2,000; selling and distribution overheads: fixed 3,000.

Prepare (a) a profit statement using **direct (marginal) costing**; (b) a statement of **marginal contribution** per metre.
answer:
**(a) Profit statement (direct costing)**

| | N | N |
|---|---|---|
| Sales (4,000 × 25) | | 100,000 |
| Less variable costs: direct materials | 18,000 | |
| variable wages | 8,000 | |
| variable factory overhead | 8,000 | |
| variable establishment charges | 2,000 | 36,000 |
| **Contribution** | | **64,000** |
| Less fixed costs: wages | 6,000 | |
| factory overhead | 2,000 | |
| establishment charges | 6,000 | |
| selling and distribution | 3,000 | 17,000 |
| **Net profit** | | **47,000** |

**(b) Marginal contribution per metre**

| | N |
|---|---|
| Selling price | 25.00 |
| Variable cost (36,000 ÷ 4,000) | 9.00 |
| **Contribution per metre** | **16.00** |

C/S ratio = 16 ÷ 25 = **64%**; break-even = 17,000 ÷ 16 = **1,062.5 metres** (N26,563 sales).

> [!answer]
> Contribution N64,000 (N16 per metre); net profit **N47,000**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Marginal costing charges only variable costs to products; all fixed costs are written off against total contribution. (The fixed and variable splits given are used; the printed headline totals in the paper don't match their components.)

## Simplified explanation

Sales − variable = contribution; − fixed = profit.
hint: Separate variable from fixed costs first.

body:
Sobea Construction Ltd secured a contract to build a swimming pool for **D275,000**, starting 1 July 2006, due in 18 months. Expenditure to 31 December 2006 (D): plant at site 125,000; stores from warehouse 320; materials purchased: cement 4,600, reinforced rods 9,200, sand 2,720; fuel for bulldozers 2,970; wages paid 13,660; wages accrued 520; employer's social security contribution 1,800; insurance 400; miscellaneous expenses 30,200.

Work certified to 15 December 2006: **D80,000**; cost of work done since (uncertified): **D7,000**. Payments are subject to **15% retention** and all money due has been received. At 31 December 2006: plant valued at **D106,000**, materials on site **D1,750**.

Prepare the contract account for the year ended 31 December 2006.
answer:
**Contract account**

| Dr | D | Cr | D |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plant at site | 125,000 | Plant c/d | 106,000 |
| Stores from warehouse | 320 | Materials on site c/d | 1,750 |
| Materials (4,600 + 9,200 + 2,720) | 16,520 | Work certified | 80,000 |
| Fuel | 2,970 | Work uncertified | 7,000 |
| Wages (13,660 + 520) | 14,180 | | |
| Social security | 1,800 | | |
| Insurance | 400 | | |
| Miscellaneous | 30,200 | | |
| **Notional profit c/d** | **3,360** | | |
| | **194,750** | | **194,750** |

Cost of work done = 191,390 − 106,000 − 1,750 = **83,640**; value of work done = 80,000 + 7,000 = 87,000; notional profit = **3,360**.

Cash received = 85% × 80,000 = **D68,000**. Work certified is 80,000 ÷ 275,000 ≈ 29% of the contract (between ¼ and ½ complete), so the usual prudence rule applies:

Profit to P&L = ⅓ × 3,360 × 68,000 ÷ 80,000 = **D952**; reserve carried forward = 3,360 − 952 = **D2,408**.

> [!answer]
> Notional profit **D3,360**; profit taken to P&L **D952**; reserve **D2,408**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

On an incomplete contract, only part of the notional profit is recognised, scaled by stage of completion and cash received.

## Simplified explanation

Costs in, valuations out; take ⅓ × cash/certified of notional profit.
hint: Include accrued wages; carry down plant and materials.
